newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK PSBR to head back into red in August.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK PSBR to head back into red in August.

text.p: Britain's public sector accounts will move firmly back into deficit in August having produced a debt repayment in July, analysts said on Monday.
A Reuter poll of economists forecast a public sector borrowing requirement of 4.1 billion stg in August, compared with a repayment of 1.7 billion in July.
However, as July saw a flood of corporation tax receipts swell the government's coffers, a PSBR of around four billion stg would compare favourably with a 4.6 billion deficit in August last year.
"The annual comparison in the fiscal deficit is likely to benefit from the echo of a high deficit figure in August last year," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
He said the cumulative deficit for the financial year so far, excluding privatisation proceeds, is likely to be nearly two billion stg below its year ago level.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said government spending was overshooting budget plans. "Perhaps that's not surprising in what is after all an election year."
But he said greater than expected strength in tax receipts, particularly value added tax (VAT), was at least partially offsetting the damage of high spending levels.
Philpotts forecast a PSBR of 4.2 billion stg in August.

Although, July's PSBR provided welcome relief after above-forecast deficit figures in the first three months of the financial year, analysts remain uncertain that the Treasury's revised PSBR forecast for the 1996/97 financial year will be hit.
The forecast is for a total PSBR of 27 billion stg.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said July's PSBR showed the effect that the British economic recovery was having on government receipts.

"Although government spending growth is running well ahead of forecasts, we expect this to be restrained as the fiscal year progresses," he said. "Indeed, we expect the government's PSBR target to be met."
Philpotts, on the other hand, expected some overshoot of the government's target.
Analysts at HSBC James Capel said the 27 billion stg forecast would be met and would allow Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to cut taxes in his November budget.
"The government is bang on target to meet its full-year projection," they said in a client note. "This still leaves open the possibility of tax cuts in November's budget."

With the Conservative government facing elections by May 1997 and trailing the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls, Clarke will be under severe pressure to deliver a budget that will lure voters the government's way.
